chat.text: Tell me what happened, in your own words. Who is the other side? What did you agree? What went wrong, and when? How much do you want back? I will ask if anything is missing.

Mark contracted seafood supplier Uncle Seng Seafood to supply 1,000 kg of premium yellowtail fish for an upcoming Grassroots dinner. The parties agreed on a locked budget of S$5,000 at a rate of S$5 per kg. Mark paid an upfront deposit of S$2,000 via UEN transfer on 12 September 2026, with the remaining balance of S$3,000 set to be paid upon delivery on 8 October 2026.  The agreement broke down on 28 September 2026 when Uncle Seng informed Mark that yellowtail was out of stock and offered to substitute it with parang fish. Mark rejected the swap because event menus specifying yellowtail had already been printed. Uncle Seng then stated that sourcing yellowtail from Malaysia would increase the price to S$6.50 per kg, raising the total cost to S$6,500, or that he would only deliver a reduced quantity of 769 kg for the original S$5,000 budget. On 1 October 2026, Mark insisted on the original contract terms or a full refund, but Uncle Seng refused to return the deposit, claiming Mark was the party cancelling. As a result, Mark had to source the required 1,000 kg of yellowtail from an emergency replacement supplier, Ah Huat, at a higher cost of S$7,000.  Mark is seeking a total claim of S$4,000. This consists of a full S$2,000 refund of the original deposit paid to Uncle Seng, plus S$2,000 in damages to cover the extra expense incurred by purchasing emergency stock from the replacement supplier.
You say the seafood supplier refused to refund your deposit or deliver as agreed. What is your full name and address, with postal code? What is the supplier's full address, with postal code?

mark tan from tampines st 99 657389

supplier is uncle seng from pasir ris st 99 282747
Who are you claiming against? What is their full address, and are they in Singapore?
supplier is uncle seng from pasir ris st 99 282747 they are in singapore
I have enough details about your claim against Uncle Seng Seafood. Now add the order, payment records, messages, and photos on the right.
apologies, uncle seng is from malaysia
The seller is outside Singapore. The tribunal cannot serve a claim outside Singapore. The Magistrate's Court can serve outside Singapore. Ask the court registry. Tell me if I have that wrong.

You are claiming $40,000. The limit is $20,000, or $30,000 if both sides agree. The seller is outside Singapore. The tribunal cannot serve a claim outside Singapore. A claim over the limit goes to the Magistrate's Court (up to $60,000) or the District Court. Tell me if I have that wrong.

scta_schedule.title: Small Claims Tribunals Act 1984, s 5(1) and the Schedule (specified claims)

scta_s2.title: Small Claims Tribunals Act 1984, s 2(1) (prescribed limit) and s 5(3)-(4)

scta_s5_time.title: Small Claims Tribunals Act 1984, s 5(3)(b) (2-year limit)
scta_s5_time.quote:
5.—(3) Except where this Act expressly provides otherwise, the jurisdiction of a tribunal does not extend to a claim —
(a) the value of which exceeds the prescribed limit; or
(b) after the expiry of 2 years after the date on which the cause of action accrued.
scta_s5_time.guide: State Courts, A Guide to Small Claims, p.4: "All claims must be filed within two years after the date the cause of action accrued. A cause of action is the fact or facts which entitles you, in law, to start a court action against the Respondent. You may file a claim in the civil courts, e.g. at the Magistrates' Courts if the cause of action accrued more than 2 years ago."

scta_s5_service.title: Small Claims Tribunals Act 1984, s 5(1)(b) (served in Singapore)
scta_s5_service.quote:
5.—(1) Subject to the provisions of this Act, a tribunal has the jurisdiction to hear and determine any claim which —
(a) is a specified claim; and
(b) is served in Singapore on the respondent under section 19(1).
scta_s5_service.guide: Judiciary, Cases eligible for a small claim: the tribunals cannot hear a claim where the respondent is outside Singapore, because the claim cannot be served on anyone outside Singapore.

blindspots.intro: Things the seller may bring that are not in your files yet. We list them so you are not surprised at the first court meeting. Answer each one.
blindspots.note: The seller can make a claim back against you, up to 3 days before the first court meeting. Your evidence list is your answer to it.

questions.q: Could the seller have a signed delivery note or an inspection record?
questions.hint: Check what you signed on delivery.

questions.q: Did the listing or terms say the goods were sold as seen, used, or without warranty?
questions.hint: Re-read the listing and any terms page.

questions.q: Did you tell the seller about the fault within a reasonable time, in writing?
questions.hint: Find the first message where you raised it and its date.

questions.q: Did anyone else use, repair or open the goods before you complained?
questions.hint: The seller may say the fault came later.

questions.q: Did anyone else see the goods when they arrived or when the fault showed?
questions.hint: Write down their name. You can name them as a witness later.

questions.q: Did you accept a partial refund, repair or replacement, even in passing?
questions.hint: If yes, say what and when. It changes the amount you claim.
